title: Most Haunted Places in Dallas-Fort Worth You Need to Know
excerpt: Discover the most haunted places in Dallas-Fort Worth, from spooky hotels and cemeteries to haunted lakes, theaters and theme parks.
content:
If you’ve lived in the DFW area for any length of time, you’re probably accustomed to hearing stories of the paranormal. From Arlington to Fort Worth and Dallas, there are countless ghost stories and legends that have been passed down for generations.

TRENDING: Top 10 Haunted Houses In The United States

From haunted lakes and cemeteries to historic hotels and even haunted theme parks, Dallas-Fort Worth is a real ghost hunter’s paradise.

TRENDING: Spooktacular Scares: Top Haunted House Thrills in DFW

Whether you’re a believer in the supernatural or simply love a good spooky story, these are some of the most haunted places across DFW that have been surrounded by mysterious sightings, unexplained activity and paranormal legends for years.

GOATMAN’S BRIDGE, DENTON

Goatman’s Bridge, also known as the Old Alton Bridge, has a long history of creepy and mysterious happenings dating back to the 1930s.

According to a long-held belief, a half-goat, half-man creature lives near the bridge and terrorizes people who visit the area. It is believed to be the ghost of a local goat farmer who was lynched on the bridge by the KKK.

Following the lynching, people have claimed over the years that mysterious disappearances have occurred when visitors go to the bridge at night. Many attribute the disappearances and the overwhelming feeling of fear and discomfort to the spirit of the Goatman. Others also believe that a young woman haunts the bridge while searching for her missing child.

Goatman’s Bridge has also been featured on numerous paranormal television shows, which has reportedly led to even more paranormal activity in the area.

SONS OF HERMANN HALL, DALLAS

Sons of Hermann Hall was established in 1910 when four independent lodges joined together to form one large, united lodge. The Hall officially held its grand opening in 1911.

Throughout its more than 100-year history, Sons of Hermann Hall has served as a gathering place for a variety of activities, most notably music and swing dancing lessons. The Hall remains open to the public today, welcoming visitors for drinks, live music, swing dancing, and other entertainment.

However, visitors should also be prepared for the possibility of encountering spirits from the Hall’s past. People have reported hearing children laughing when no children were present and seeing the former caretaker, a loving couple, and patrons dressed in their finest as if they were preparing to attend concerts from the past. Visitors have also reported hearing doors slam and witnessing paintings randomly fall from the walls.

W.E SCOTT THEATRE, FORT WORTH

The theatre is believed to be haunted by Mr. Scott himself, who has reportedly been spotted on several occasions. According to the stories, he appears to still be keeping an eye on his investment, often straightening pictures that have been left hanging crooked.

Related Stories

Mr. Scott is said to be joined by another ghost, believed to be the spirit of Kenneth Walker, a stagehand who hanged himself in the prop room in 1970. Walker is reportedly seen wearing a brown suit as he walks across the stage and has also been heard laughing from underneath it.

SIX FLAGS OVER TEXAS, ARLINGTON

Six Flags Over Texas was the idea of Texas oilman Angus G. Wynne, Jr., who wanted to create a theme park that would surpass Disneyland in size while being accessible to more people. With that vision, he opened Six Flags Over Texas in 1961.

The theme park offers a variety of rides and activities, but supernatural experiences are among the least expected. Ghosts have reportedly been spotted in several areas throughout the park, including the Candy Store, Music Mill, Palace, and open areas such as the Log Ride.

One of the park’s most famous ghosts is a little girl named Annie, who is said to spend her time at the Candy Store. According to the stories, another girl died at age 8 after drowning in Johnson’s Creek. Her ghost is said to visit an old farmhouse that now sits within the park and walk along the local railroad tracks.

Other reported paranormal activity includes lights turning on and off, curtains opening, doors slamming shut, and doors that will not remain locked. Employees have also reportedly experienced the sensation of being touched and unexplained cold spots.

FORT WORTH ZOO, FORT WORTH

The Fort Worth Zoo is considered one of the top five zoos in the United States and, despite hosting regular “spooky sleepovers,” only a handful of people know that the zoo is believed to be one of the most haunted locations in Fort Worth.

The zoo is reportedly haunted by former animal trainer Michael A. Bell, who was crushed to death by a four-ton bull elephant in 1987 while attempting to move the elephant and two females into a larger enclosure. The male elephant reportedly asserted himself as the dominant male, crushing Bell in the process.

Since the tragic accident, visitors have reported seeing the ghostly apparition of a man walking near the elephant and zebra exhibits. Bell is reportedly not the only spirit said to haunt the zoo. There have also been numerous reports of a woman dressed in 19th-century white clothing, carrying a parasol and pacing back and forth in front of the zoo café. Her identity remains unknown, but her spirit is reportedly seen regularly.

MILLERMORE HOUSE, DALLAS HERITAGE VILLAGE, DALLAS

Dallas Heritage Village is home to a collection of Victorian and 19th-century pioneer homes, with some buildings dating back to the 1800s.

The Millermore Mansion is known for its impressive size and design, but it is also associated with reports of paranormal activity. People have reported seeing a female ghost near the sickroom and nursery on the second floor of the Millermore. Guests and employees have also reported unusual and sudden drops in temperature inside the nursery.

With many people dying from infectious diseases such as smallpox, diphtheria, and pneumonia before vaccinations were available, it is understandable that their spirits could remain.

It has also been noted that spirits connected to gang murder in the 1920s are reportedly found in the Law Office Building.

ARTISAN CENTER THEATRE, ARLINGTON

The Artisan Center Theatre is technically located in Hurst, just a few miles from Arlington, but it is still considered a nearby location. Originally known as the Belaire Theatre, it is said to be haunted by the spirit of a former employee who died of a heart attack while on duty.

The former projectionist is reportedly not the only spirit in the theatre. There have also been sightings of a young female ghost, with several people claiming to have actually interacted with her. Another male spirit named Neil is also said to haunt the theatre and is described as being particularly unfriendly.

The theatre has also been the site of frequent reports of unexplained sounds, disembodied voices, faucets turning on and off by themselves, and flickering lights.

OLD HERON CASTLE, FORT WORTH

The castle was rebuilt on the shore of Lake Worth by one of its former owners and is said to be haunted by the spirit of a young man who is often seen wandering around the castle grounds. There have also been occasional reports of him appearing inside the castle.

Another reported spirit is Lake Worth’s “Runaway Bride.” Visitors have claimed to see the ghostly bride running across the entrance road leading up to the castle before she suddenly disappears.

RIVER LEGACY PARK, ARLINGTON

River Legacy Park is home to several reportedly haunted hotspots, with at least two locations known for their own paranormal tales.

The first is “Hell’s Gate,” a long trail surrounded by thick swamps and large trees. Local legend claims that captured Union Army spies were taken along this trail to be hanged. Near Hell’s Gate, a red-haired apparition dressed in a Confederate General’s uniform is reportedly seen walking along a narrow path. Some people have also reported hearing moaning coming from the side of the trail.

Another reportedly haunted location is Screaming Bridge. According to its history, a car carrying a group of kids was involved in a fatal accident while crossing the Trinity River on a narrow bridge. The bridge is now open only to foot traffic, but the spirits of those who died in the accident are said to remain. Witnesses have reported that walking the trail at night may reveal apparitions of tombstones in the water, with one tombstone said to represent each of the deaths.

THISTLE HILL, FORT WORTH

Thistle Hill dates back to around 1903, when it was built for Ms. Electra Waggoner Wharton, the daughter of wealthy rancher and oilman William “Tom” Waggoner.

Today, the historic residence serves as a venue for private events, while tours are also available.

Stories of Thistle Hill being haunted did not begin until the 1970s, when renovation work on the property is believed to have disturbed spirits that were resting there. Since then, two apparitions have reportedly been spotted regularly around the property.

A lady in white is said to appear on the landing of the main grand staircase, while another apparition is described as a gentleman wearing tennis clothes and sporting a handlebar mustache. Visitors have also reported hearing phantom music coming from the ballroom, along with phantom footsteps and disembodied voices.

LOST CEMETERY OF INFANTS, ARLINGTON

In 1894, society viewed unmarried mothers very differently, with many considered social outcasts and shunned by “polite society.” This led Reverend James Tony Upchurch to establish the Berachah Industrial Home for the Redemption and Protection of Erring Girls.

The home provided young “fallen” women with the opportunity to learn useful workplace skills so they could eventually rejoin society after giving birth. Over time, the institution developed into a largely self-sufficient village.

By 1935, the institution had become an orphanage, presumably for the children of these women. Today, the only remaining part of the property is a graveyard known as the Lost Cemetery of Infants.

Most of the graves belong to stillborn children or infants who died shortly after birth due to complications or birth defects. The cemetery is fairly hidden, but people who have found it have described seeing shadowy figures moving between the trees and feeling as though they were being watched.

There have also been reports of disembodied children’s voices and instances of small toys appearing or disappearing from the graves.

LA QUINTA INN & SUITES, DALLAS DOWNTOWN (FORMERLY THE HOTEL LAWRENCE)

When La Quinta Inn & Suites first opened in 1925, it was known as the Scott Hotel and initially served people traveling into the city through Union Station. Over time, the hotel underwent many changes and became a popular destination.

Throughout its history, the hotel has been the site of several instances of violence, including multiple murders and deaths. One of the reported ghosts is a murder victim named Jack “Smiley” Jackson. According to the story, he will hold the door to room 1009 shut unless he is politely asked to move. Another man was also reportedly killed in the same room when his throat was cut.

Additional deaths at the hotel include a congressman who committed suicide and a woman who either fell or was pushed from the tenth floor. With so many deaths reported at the hotel, people have claimed to see ghosts, hear footsteps, and witness objects moving on their own.

ARLINGTON MUSIC HALL, ARLINGTON

Arlington Music Hall is reportedly haunted by a resident spirit nicknamed Fred.

The venue’s former owner, Jean Collins, says she has heard an invisible presence moving around the stage. She has also experienced lights turning back on after being completely switched off, something many of her employees have reportedly experienced as well.

Fred is said to extend beyond the music hall. The owner of the neighboring Babe’s Chicken Dinner House claims to have seen Fred wandering around the restaurant on occasion. On one occasion, Fred reportedly approached the owner and told him that he used to live there.

Fred is considered to be a friendly spirit who does not mean any harm. During a paranormal investigation, a female voice was reportedly captured as an EVP saying that Fred is a good man.

MAJESTIC THEATER, DALLAS

The Majestic Theater opened its doors on April 11, 1921, and was once home to vaudeville performers and other notable figures, including Bob Hope, Harry Houdini, Mae West, and Jack Benny.

The theater eventually closed for renovations before reopening as a venue for a variety of entertainment, including plays, concerts, and comedy acts.

The Majestic is also associated with several reported paranormal occurrences. Visitors have reported hearing doors opening and closing, footsteps when no one is around, and lights turning on without explanation. Others have reported seeing shadows and noticing unusual or unexplained fragrances throughout the theater.

WHITE ROCK LAKE & FLAG POLE HILL, DALLAS

Flag Pole Hill is an area near Dallas that, according to local legend, is best avoided at night when possible.

One of the area’s most well-known ghost stories involves a young woman who reportedly stopped a passing driver and asked for a ride home. When the driver arrived at the woman’s home, she was nowhere to be found, and all that remained in the back seat was a puddle of water. When the driver knocked on the door to ask about the woman, an older man answered. After the driver described the girl, the man confirmed that she was his daughter but explained that she had died many years earlier after tragically drowning in White Rock Lake.

There have also been numerous reports of rocks being thrown at cars traveling on the road from Flag Pole Hill. Some people have even claimed that ghosts have struck cars while they were driving.

The cause of the reported haunting at Flag Pole Hill is debated. Some connect it to a past slaughter of Native Americans on the land, while others believe it is connected to murder-suicides that occurred near White Rock Lake and Blackbird Lane.

MISS MOLLY’S HOTEL, FORTH WORTH STOCKYARDS

Miss Molly’s Hotel has long been considered one of the most haunted locations in Fort Worth. The bed and breakfast is located in the heart of Fort Worth’s historic Stockyards and attracts a mix of Wild West romantics and paranormal enthusiasts.

The hotel originally opened in 1910 as an upscale boarding house called The Palace Rooms. It later became a speakeasy during Prohibition before eventually falling on hard times and operating as a bordello.

In recent years, Miss Molly’s has become increasingly known as a haunted location, with reports of several tragic entities dating back to the 1940s and 1950s. Most of the reported spirits are women, including murdered prostitutes and a woman who died from lung disease. According to visiting mediums, none of the women appeared to be aware that they had died.

Guests have reported seeing beautiful female spirits appear at the foot of their beds, particularly in the Cattlemen’s Room. There are also reports of a young girl who is believed to have died from typhoid in the 19th century.

BAKER HOTEL, MINERAL WELLS

The Baker Hotel, featuring more than 400 rooms across 14 floors, opened its doors to the public in 1929. The hotel offered guests a place to relax, with spa-like treatments, massages, food, and beverages.

Throughout the 1930s, 1940s, and 1950s, the Baker welcomed many famous entertainers and notable figures, including Helen Keller, Judy Garland, Will Rogers, Sammy Kaye, and even Bonnie and Clyde. The hotel also witnessed many deaths during its history, which has contributed to reports of paranormal activity.

One common occurrence is the appearance of orbs in photographs taken at the Baker. Housekeepers have also reportedly found glasses with red lipstick stains in unoccupied rooms.

Visitors have claimed to see the ghost of a little boy in a wheelchair, as well as the ghost of a woman known as the Lady in White.

THE ADOLPHUS HOTEL, DALLAS

As Dallas experienced a period of growth and prosperity, there was a need for a grand hotel, and Adolphus Busch helped bring that vision to life. By 1912, The Adolphus Hotel had opened its doors to the public.

Throughout its history, the hotel has welcomed royalty, presidents, business moguls, and other famous individuals. While The Adolphus is known for its opulence, guests and employees have also reported paranormal activity over the years.

People have reported feeling as though they are being followed or watched when no one is around, as well as feeling someone tap them on the shoulder when no one is nearby. Others have reported seeing windows suddenly fly open, hearing doors slam, and hearing footsteps outside their rooms when no one is in the hallway.

On the 19th floor, people have reportedly seen the spirit of a woman who is said to have hanged herself after her fiancé failed to show up for their wedding ceremony. Guests have also reported hearing the sound of the same woman crying.
